summary: Comprehensive OWASP Top-10 review of the Task 8 HTTP layer (BotController + ConnectBotRequest + BotResponse + integration tests). The implementation is correctly defended on every dimension specifically called out by user-spec (AC2/AC10/AC11/AC16/AC17/AC18/AC20/AC23) and the tech-spec security decisions (R1/D1/D2/D14/D16/D17). Token never appears in any response shape; encrypted-token fields are JsonIgnored on the entity AND absent from the response record AND assertively re-checked at build time by BotTokenLeakTest; mass-assignment is blocked by @JsonIgnoreProperties + the controller deriving ownerId from the security context (never from the body); the bean-validation regex short-circuits malformed tokens at the WebExchangeBindException layer with a 400 before BotService runs (verified by AC2 test asserting MockWebServer records zero requests on a malformed body); anti-enumeration collapses foreign / soft-deleted / malformed projectId all to identical 404s through ProjectService.requireOwned which is the first reactive step on every endpoint; brute-force counter (D14) is integrated, fail-open is observable through a pinned WARN line, and the counter trips BEFORE any Telegram call; audit-event metadata is the closed key set {projectId, telegramBotId, telegramUsername} for bot_connected and {projectId, telegramBotId, webhookDeleted} for bot_disconnected with no token-shaped values; ipAddress / userAgent are stored as top-level Event fields outside the metadata bag; CSRF + auth are correctly delegated to the WebFlux SecurityConfig (controller declares no permitAll path); error responses are routed through GlobalErrorHandler which never echoes the request body. No hardcoded secrets. No SQL/NoSQL injection surface (no user-controlled query strings; Mongo lookups are by typed parameters). No SSRF (the only outbound URL is the configured Telegram base URL composed with the bot token in the path, not user-controlled URLs). No insecure deserialization (Jackson on a record with explicit @JsonIgnoreProperties + @Pattern). One info-level observation: extractIp blindly trusts X-Forwarded-For — this is a PLATFORM-LEVEL concern shared verbatim with ProjectController/ProfileController, NOT a task-8 regression, and should be tracked at the deployment / reverse-proxy layer (must strip/validate XFF before traffic reaches the app). No critical/high/medium findings; one informational note for traceability.

findings.owasp_category: A09: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
findings.issue: extractIp() blindly trusts the first X-Forwarded-For value with no upstream-proxy validation. Identical to ProjectController/ProfileController so this is a platform-level pattern, not a task-8 regression. The IP value lands in the bot_connected / bot_disconnected audit events (Event.ipAddress top-level field). An authenticated user (or a misconfigured deployment that exposes the app port directly to the internet without a trusted reverse proxy) can spoof the audit ip by sending a forged X-Forwarded-For header; this would not gain privileges but would corrupt forensic accuracy for security incidents involving Connect/Disconnect. Brute-force keying is per-userId so this does NOT enable rate-limit bypass. Not a task-8 fix; document the trust boundary.
findings.suggested_fix: Document the deployment expectation that the reverse proxy MUST strip incoming X-Forwarded-For and append only its own observed peer IP (e.g. nginx: real_ip_header X-Forwarded-For; set_real_ip_from <proxy CIDR>; or platform-equivalent on the chosen host). Long-term: add an app.proxy.trusted-proxies allowlist consulted by extractIp — but as a single platform-wide refactor across BotController + ProjectController + ProfileController, not in this task. For task 8 this is acknowledged-and-deferred.
